raw_response.blind_rationale: This study directly evaluates the household-level service-access impact of urban water utility privatization in Bolivia (the 1997 30-year private concession to Aguas del Illimani S.A. in La Paz and El Alto, regulated by SISAB with contractual in-house connection mandates, 5-year expansion targets, and regulated tariffs/connection fees) compared against non-privatized municipal public provision (Cochabamba) and cooperative provision (Santa Cruz de la Sierra). Narrow Criterion 2 is clearly met (`yes_rule_mechanism`) because utility ownership/concession regime and regulatory contract rules directly govern service expansion and connection terms. Criterion 4 is clearly met (`yes_household_or_service_access`) because the primary econometric outcome is a household-level binary indicator for piped water access inside the dwelling/yard from the utility network (supplemented by descriptive coverage, equity concentration indices, and household water affordability at the >3% income threshold). Under SWiM taxonomy, private concession vs. public/cooperative utility ownership belongs squarely in `Family C` (ownership, regulation, institutional capacity, administrative structure), with clear directionality (positive long-run 1996–2005 probit DID marginal effects of +0.077 and +0.075 on piped water access, p < 0.01; null short-run 1996–2001 effect of 0.025, SE = 0.025). Note: PDF text extraction drops minus signs on negative numbers in tables (e.g., Cochabamba's coverage drop and baseline dummies in Table 12), but the prose on p. 2574 (PDF p. 11) explicitly confirms that the `Effect` interaction coefficient in 1996–2005 is positive, while the short-run 1996–2001 `Effect` is statistically insignificant.

raw_response.headline_estimate_summary: Primary econometric estimate (Table 12, p. 2574 / PDF p. 11; probit DID reporting marginal effects of `Effect = post * privatized` on household piped water access): Long-run 1996 vs. 2005: (1) controlling for log per capita income (`lnY capita`) and city dummies: marginal effect = +0.077, SE = 0.016, p < 0.01 (***), N = 2,917 households (weighted pop. = 1,476,802; F(6, 2911) = 35.44); (2) controlling for dwelling wealth (`Rooms`, `Electricity`, `Wall`) and city dummies: marginal effect = +0.075, SE = 0.015, p < 0.01 (***), N = 2,945 households (weighted pop. = 1,487,615; F(8, 2937) = 31.23). Short-run 1996 vs. 2001: (1) controlling for `lnY capita` and city dummies: marginal effect = 0.025 (sign ambiguous due to PDF minus-sign stripping, |t| = 1.00), SE = 0.025, not statistically significant, N = 3,240 (F(6, 3234) = 30.41); (2) controlling for dwelling wealth and city dummies: marginal effect = 0.025, SE = 0.025, not statistically significant, N = 3,277 (F(8, 3269) = 32.84). Descriptive 1996–2005 piped-water coverage changes (Tables 5–6, pp. 2569–2570 / PDF pp. 6–7): La Paz total 87.9% to 96.6% (poorest quintile QI: +12.8 pp, p < 0.05), El Alto total 76.2% to 87.8% (QI: +30.3 pp, p < 0.05), Cochabamba total 76.5% to 61.8% (QI: -37.4 pp, p < 0.05; minus sign stripped in PDF Table 6), Santa Cruz total 95.5% to 95.6% (QI: 0.0 pp, ns). Affordability (Table 11, p. 2574 / PDF p. 11, share of connected QI households spending >3% of income on water, 2001 to 2005): La Paz 34.8% to 42.1%, El Alto 25.6% to 15.1%, Cochabamba 63.9% to 23.2%, Santa Cruz 78.4% to 73.1%.
raw_response.study_design_and_sample: Repeated cross-sectional difference-in-differences (probit DID reporting marginal effects, plus descriptive Welch t-tests, Kakwani achievement indices, concentration indices, and expenditure/affordability comparisons) in urban Bolivia across 4 cities: La Paz and El Alto (privatized via 1997 concession) vs. Santa Cruz de la Sierra (cooperative) and Cochabamba (municipal public utility). Unit of analysis: household, drawn from 4 INE household surveys: 1992 (N = 3,169), 1996 (N = 2,138), 2001 (N = 1,197), and 2005 (N = 807). Primary probit DID analytic sample sizes (Table 12): N = 3,240 and N = 3,277 households (1996 & 2001); N = 2,917 and N = 2,945 households (1996 & 2005).
